title: Measurable functions and characteristic functions
terms: measurable function; characteristic function; indicator function; pointwise limit; almost- everywhere limit.

exposition.text:
A real function is Lebesgue measurable when the inverse image of every open real set is mea-
surable. Continuous functions are measurable, as are sums, differences, products, and absolute
values of measurable functions. Pointwise limits of measurable functions are measurable; for
Lebesgue measure this remains true for almost-everywhere limits and arbitrary changes on null
sets.
The characteristic or indicator function χ equals 1 on E and 0 elsewhere. It is measurable
E
exactly when E is measurable. Its discontinuities are exactly the boundary of E, which explains
why a measurable function can be discontinuous everywhere.
Pointwise convergence requires f (x) → f(x) at every point. Almost-everywhere convergence
n
permits a measurable exceptional set of measure zero. Because Lebesgue measure includes
every subset of a null set, changing a measurable function arbitrarily on such a set preserves
measurability; it need not preserve continuity or boundedness.

question.text:
On [0, 1], set f (x) = xχ (x). At which points is f continuous?
Q
(A) Every point.
(B) Every irrational point.
(C) Every rational point.
(D) 0 only.
(E) No point.

solution.text:
At 0, |f (x)| ≤ x → 0. At any a > 0, rational inputs tending to a give values tending to
a, while irrational inputs give zero. The incompatible limits show discontinuity at every
positive point.

Let N ⊂ R have Lebesgue measure zero, and let h : N → R be arbitrary. Define f = h on N
and f = 0 outside N. Which statement must hold?
(A) f is continuous.
(B) f is bounded.
(C) f vanishes at every point.
(D) f is nonmeasurable unless h is continuous.
(E) f is Lebesgue measurable.

solution.text:
If an open target set omits zero, its inverse image under f is a subset of the null set N and
is measurable. If it contains zero, the complement of the inverse image is such a subset.
Thus f is measurable regardless of the assigned values on N. The constant sequence of zero
functions converges to f almost everywhere, although not necessarily at points of N .
